title: Release-Date Congestion Map and Collision Cover
one_liner: A wishlist-overlap model and anonymous date-slot registry that tells indies where launch windows are crowded, later backed by parametric cover if a mega-title lands on top of them.
customer: Self-publishing indie developers and small publishers with 20k+ wishlists, and later insurers and MGAs underwriting launch risk.
problem: GTA VI launches 2026-11-19, and other publishers are rescheduling around it. Silksong (about 5.2M wishlists, 7M+ sales by Dec 2025) pushed several indies to delay after its date was announced. Devs lock marketing spend, then a giant date shifts. When everyone dodges the same date, they pile into the same safe windows, creating new collisions.
solution: Ingest public Steam wishlist ranks, release calendars and creator schedules to produce a congestion map and a per-title collision score based on audience overlap. Add a confidential slot registry where publishers submit intended dates and get congestion feedback. Once loss data exists, add parametric cover paying out if a listed mega-title moves within +/-14 days of a locked date.
why_now: GTA VI is the largest release-calendar shock in years and its ripple lasts months. Q1 2027 herd behavior is forming now, and no one measures collision risk.
revenue_model: $49-299 per month SaaS or $500 per date report, plus a 15-25% MGA commission on parametric premiums (3-6% of cover).
non_obvious_insight: Collision is treated as luck, but it is measurable through audience overlap and tradeable as a parametric risk. The herd effect, everyone avoiding the same date, is a coordination failure a neutral registry can fix.
first_30_days: Scrape Steam release calendars and wishlist ranks. Publish a free Q1 2027 congestion map on Discord and Reddit dev communities. Sell 20 paid date reports and speak to 3 MGAs about a pilot cover.

title: Managed Runtime for Custom Apps Built for Local Businesses
one_liner: A white-label hosting, backup and "someone to call" layer for AI-built custom apps that freelancers and owners now build for small businesses.
customer: Two buyers. (a) Solo builders, freelancers and small agencies who build custom tools for local businesses, including failed micro-SaaS founders. They pay wholesale per app and mark it up. (b) Small business owners who built a tool themselves and want it kept alive.
problem: Builders and buyers have both moved off subscription SaaS, and reliability is now nobody's job. r/SaaS: "Customer cancelled after 18 months. Reason: 'We built it ourselves.'", "No one is going to pay for your vibe-coded SaaS", "Mass-produced AI apps for 14 months. Made $2,847 total. My friend sells pool cleaning services and cleared $94K.", "I wasted $50k because I thought the code was the expensive part." r/Entrepreneur (88/100): "The SaaS model is quietly falling apart for small businesses." When the dispatch board or intake form breaks at 7am, nobody is answerable.
solution: 1) A one-click deploy of an AI-built app to a hardened runtime with auth, nightly backups, uptime checks, data export and secrets rotation. 2) Dependency and security patching. 3) A "break-glass" human fix within one business day, sold as credits. 4) Builders resell the bundle with their own markup, so they earn recurring revenue from boring customers instead of chasing SaaS signups. 5) The small business gets an SLA and a runbook in plain language.
why_now: In February 2026 nearly $1T was wiped from software and services valuations as coding agents made build-versus-buy tilt toward build (TechCrunch, Mar 1, 2026). Small customers are now building their own replacements, and thousands of AI-SaaS founders who cannot sell subscriptions are turning to service-style custom work.
revenue_model: $39-79 per app per month wholesale to builders, who charge clients $100-200/mo. Break-glass fix credits ($150 per incident). A $199/mo direct plan for owners who built their own tool.
non_obvious_insight: When code is cheap, the scarce thing is accountability: someone who answers when the tool breaks. The supply and demand are visible in the same threads: small customers churn because they built it themselves (r/SaaS, https://www.ideafast.pro/pains/saas), and r/Entrepreneur scores "The SaaS model is quietly falling apart for small businesses" at 88/100 (https://www.ideafast.pro/pains/Entrepreneur). The macro shift toward build over buy is documented at https://techcrunch.com/2026/03/01/saas-in-saas-out-heres-whats-driving-the-saaspocalypse/. Honest caveat: the demand for the caretaking layer is inferred from these signals, not seen in a direct "I'd pay for" post, so the first month is a paid-demand test.
first_30_days: Week 1: DM 30 builders who posted about pivoting to "boring" service customers, and offer to host and maintain their existing client apps for $49. Weeks 2-3: onboard 10 real apps onto a standard stack (managed database, backups, uptime monitor, alerts) using off-the-shelf tooling. Week 4: sell the wholesale plan to the first 3 builders and log every incident to price break-glass credits. Kill test: fewer than 5 paying apps after 30 days means the pain is not there.

title: Human Callback Line Sold Through Credit Unions
one_liner: A staffed 'is this really my grandson?' phone line and call-screening kit for members over 70, paid for per enrolled member by community credit unions whose deposits walk out the door in voice-clone scams.
customer: Community banks and credit unions with $300M-$5B in assets and an older membership, paying about $3-6 per enrolled member per month. A secondary direct-to-family tier is $12 per month paid by adult children.
problem: Voice cloning needs only a few seconds of audio, and older adults are losing large sums to family-emergency and impersonation scams. The FBI reportedly counted about $352M in AI-linked fraud losses among people over 60 in 2025, and the FTC estimates most fraud goes unreported. Victims are shamed and rushed, and the scam's whole design is to prevent a pause. Most transfers are authorized, so banks are usually not liable, but the member's savings leave the institution and often end up in a crypto ATM.
solution: A screen-free service: one memorable number on a fridge magnet and phone sticker. Whenever anyone calls asking for money or urgency, the member hangs up and calls the line. A trained human (retired tellers, 911 dispatchers, nurses) runs a slow 5-minute out-of-band check: pre-registered family safe word, a call-back to the real relative through their stored circle, and a plain-language 'this matches a known scam script' verdict. Members with large cash withdrawals or wires get a teller prompt that says 'want to call the line first?', with the credit union's flag visible to the desk. Enrollment happens at branches and senior centers with a 20-minute family safe-word ritual.
why_now: Voice-clone scams have moved from novelty to mainstream in 2025-26. Regulators, state elder-exploitation reporting duties and the UK's mandatory reimbursement rules for authorized push-payment fraud point the direction US institutions are heading. Credit unions are competing on trust and member service against fintech, and have no good product for the fraud they cannot block.
revenue_model: B2B2C per-enrolled-member fee ($3-6 per month) with a pilot flat fee of about $2,000 per month per credit union; overage for call volume; $12 per month direct-to-family plan; optional add-on to sell to insurers of members' homes and autos.
non_obvious_insight: Against a perfect fake voice, the only durable defense is a slow, human, out-of-band ritual, and the buyer is not the senior but the institution holding the money. The scam is a deposit-flight event, and credit unions have the branch relationship, field-of-membership community ties and senior-center access to reach victims before the scammer does. Making the 'moment of doubt' land on a number people already trust is cheaper than any AI detector.
first_30_days: Pitch one sub-$1B credit union through its CEO or member-experience lead (reach them via state credit union league events and CUNA meetups). Recruit 8 retired tellers and dispatchers to staff phone shifts from home using Twilio and a shared inbox, with no engineering needed. Enroll 60 seniors from a local senior center in a 60-day pilot and log every attempted scam reported. Sell the results as a member-perk pilot at $2,000 per month.

title: Tele-Clearance for Sheriffs' Booking Desks
one_liner: A night-shift nurse-and-NP screening service that lets a rural deputy clear an arrestee for booking from the jail, without spending four hours in the ER while the county goes unpatrolled.
customer: County sheriffs and county commissioners, funded through county risk pools and insurers (for example state association-of-counties liability pools) that pay for jail deaths and lawsuits. Paid per county per month.
problem: Rural jails often have no on-site medical staff, so jail policy requires a hospital 'medical clearance' for any arrestee who is intoxicated, injured or says his chest hurts. At 2am the deputy brings the person to the ER and sits with him for 3-5 hours, sometimes the county's only deputy on duty. The county pays a $2,000-4,000 ER bill and has nobody patrolling. The ER meanwhile holds a bed and a nurse for someone with nothing acutely wrong except being drunk. When clearance is skipped, the risk is a death in custody from alcohol or opioid withdrawal, a head injury or diabetic crisis, which is a lawsuit.
solution: A booking-desk kit (vitals, pulse oximeter, glucometer, breathalyzer, tablet) plus 24/7 on-demand video screening by an RN and NP working from home, using a physician-signed clearance protocol built from ACEP's published best-practice guidance for patients in custody. Dispositions are 'fit for booking with monitoring plan', 'needs ER now', or 're-check in 2 hours'. The service also creates a documented withdrawal-watch checklist, such as sobriety and CIWA-style monitoring, which jails need for liability reasons. The report is time-stamped and defensible.
why_now: Rural hospital and ER closures are lengthening transport times. Prison Policy Initiative reported in October 2025 that about half of incarcerated people are held in rural jails and prisons that risk losing hospital access. Medicaid cuts and the pressure on county budgets are also forcing sheriffs to look for cheaper options, and some already release people on 'medical bond' to avoid ER bills. Telehealth billing and licensure flexibility, together with the Nurse Licensure Compact, make cross-state night staffing workable.
revenue_model: $2,000-3,500 per county per month, including up to about 40 screens. Additional screens are $85 each. Roughly 12 counties would support a team of 6 part-time clinicians. Later, sell an outcome dashboard called 'deputy hours returned to patrol', which is the number commissioners and risk-pool underwriters will care about most.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone frames the problem as ER wait time or inmate healthcare. From inside the ER, the real cost is the deputy who is stuck with us. In a county with one or two deputies on at night, an ER trip is a public safety hole, and the buyer will pay to close it. Also, most 'medical clearances' are defensive medicine that a good screen would make unnecessary. Big correctional health vendors (Wellpath, NaphCare) sell staffing for large jails and are not built for a 12-bed jail on a county road.
first_30_days: Write the clearance protocol with a supervising physician from a rural ER and get it reviewed by one county attorney. Choose one sheriff the founder already knows from ER encounters. Run a paid pilot at $1,500 for 60 days and count deputy hours saved and ER trips avoided. Then pitch the state's county risk pool and sheriffs' association with the numbers.

title: One Guide, Twelve Languages: Live-Dubbed Tours
one_liner: The guide speaks once and each guest hears their own language in low-latency synthesised audio, so mixed-language groups share one guide and cities see fewer, fuller groups.
customer: Independent guides, small tour operators and shore-excursion companies in cities that cap groups (Venice, Rome, Florence, Amsterdam, Kyoto), plus guide associations and municipalities.
problem: Language-siloed tours multiply the number of groups on the same street, and group-size caps and guide quotas bind. Guides cannot fill rare-language tours, and whisper systems only amplify the guide's voice.
solution: Guide microphone to live speech translation to each guest's phone, joined by QR with no app install, with per-listener language choice, a glossary of place names, an offline fallback, headcount tools and translated questions back to the guide. Sell a clip mic and hub kit plus per-tour credits.
why_now: Real-time speech-to-speech translation became good enough in 2025 (consumer earbuds now offer live translation and APIs offer realtime speech), eSIM and 5G make connectivity easy, and cities are tightening group caps.
revenue_model: USD 39-99 per guide per month or USD 1-2 per guest, USD 150 kits and municipal licences.
non_obvious_insight: Language silos are a hidden multiplier of overtourism. Merging groups cuts the number of groups without cutting visitors, so guides earn more and cities become allies and customers.
first_30_days: Recruit 20 guides in Rome and Florence, pilot two-language tours then four, and measure latency and guest satisfaction. Approach the guide association with the pilot results.

title: Forensic Chat-Log Analysis for AI-Harm Lawsuits
one_liner: A court-defensible method and service that turns exported chatbot transcripts into escalation timelines, sycophancy evidence and missed-crisis reports for plaintiffs, defense counsel and regulators.
customer: Plaintiff firms handling AI wrongful-death and psychosis cases, defense counsel at AI companies and app makers, and state attorneys general, paying $10-30k per case plus expert-witness fees.
problem: Trend chain: over a million weekly suicide-related conversations with general chatbots (OpenAI, Oct 2025), then Raine v. OpenAI plus at least nine similar suits, then hundreds of thousands of words of transcript per case with no standard way to measure sycophancy, delusion reinforcement or whether crisis protocols fired. Expert testimony is ad hoc, and the first Daubert-style challenges are coming.
solution: A clinician-designed coding manual plus a software pipeline. It ingests exports from ChatGPT, Character.ai and Replika formats and tags each turn for risk disclosure, model response type (refuse, validate, encourage, refer) and escalation, then produces an evidentiary report with reproducibility statistics and inter-rater reliability from two clinician coders plus model assistance.
why_now: The litigation wave is live, Pennsylvania's Department of State sued in May 2026, the Human Line Project reports members in 22 countries with logs in hand, and no accepted methodology exists yet. Whoever's method survives the first challenge becomes the standard.
revenue_model: Per-case fixed fee of $10-30k, subscriptions for firms with multiple cases, expert-witness and training fees, later insurer and state-AG contracts.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not AI. It is a validated, adversarially tested coding scheme that survives its first Daubert challenge, like DNA or forensic accounting. Because defense will need the same method, the business is side-agnostic and cannot be undercut by a lab.
first_30_days: Recruit a forensic psychiatrist and a forensic linguist. Code the excerpts quoted in five public complaints to build a v0.1 manual. Offer three plaintiff firms a free two-week pilot analysis on one case each, then convert to fixed fees and publish a methods note.

title: 1098-VLI Reporting for Small Auto Lenders
one_liner: Turn a loan tape into IRS-ready Form 1098-VLI statements, with VIN validation and U.S.-final-assembly flags, for credit unions, community banks and buy-here-pay-here dealers that cannot wait for their core vendor.
customer: Credit unions, community banks, CDFIs, independent auto finance companies, buy-here-pay-here dealers and their loan servicers. Any trade or business receiving $600 or more in interest on a qualifying vehicle loan must report, and the statute has no small-lender exemption. The lender pays per form and per VIN cleanse.
problem: Treasury's final regulations under IRC 6050AA (published Sept 8, 2026; effective Nov 9, 2026) require Form 1098-VLI showing borrower TIN, interest received, opening principal, origination date and the vehicle's year, make, model and VIN. Statements are due to borrowers by Jan 31 and to the IRS by Feb 28 (Mar 31 if e-filed), with penalties under 6721 and 6722. Transition relief covered 2025, so the 2026 tax year is the first full-form season. The preamble concedes lenders 'may need to collect additional information' and 'may experience difficulties accurately reporting the VIN'. Treasury declined to make lenders verify U.S. assembly, allowing reliance on the VIN plant code or the manufacturer's final-assembly label.
solution: The lender uploads a CSV from its core or loan origination system. The service validates VIN check digits, decodes them through NHTSA's free decoder, and maps plant-of-manufacture codes through a curated plant-to-final-assembly table it maintains. It screens for new versus used, personal use and origination date, and checks TIN completeness. It produces an exception queue (missing or wrong VINs) with borrower outreach templates. It then generates and delivers the 1098-VLI statements and e-files with the IRS. A white-label web widget for lender sites answers 'is my loan deduction-eligible?'
why_now: The regs were finalized Sept 8, 2026 and take effect Nov 9. Statements are due Jan 31, 2027, giving four months. Big core processors will serve their largest clients first, and 2026 is the first year without a simple summary-statement safe harbor. The consumer deduction (up to $10,000 of interest on new, U.S.-assembled vehicles under the 2025 tax law) means borrowers will call their lenders asking whether their car qualifies.
revenue_model: $2-4 per form with a $1,500 annual minimum. $0.25 per loan for VIN cleansing and exception handling. Enterprise license for servicers and core-vendor partners. Consumer eligibility widget with lead-gen to tax preparers or refinance offers.
non_obvious_insight: Treasury turned a bright-line rule into a data-quality problem and pushed the risk to the lender. Whether a car is American-assembled is answered by plant-code tables and labels, not by anything in a lender's servicing system, and the preamble openly warns of VIN reporting difficulties. The moat is a curated plant-to-final-assembly table plus an exceptions workflow, which the big vendors will treat as an edge case for small clients. Source: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/09/08/2026-18219/car-loan-interest-deduction (final regs on 6050AA reporting, Form 1098-VLI, the $600 threshold, no small-lender exemption, and the VIN and plant-of-manufacture provisions).
first_30_days: Build the VIN pipeline on NHTSA's free decoder and validate it on 1,000 real VINs. Offer 30 credit unions a free VIN readiness audit on a 500-loan sample tape and show them their error rate. Publish a plant-code explainer for CU and community bank newsletters. Sign three design partners through state credit union leagues and CUSOs, with a goal of $10k in prepaid annual minimums by December.

title: Fall Response Network for Meteorite Hunters
one_liner: Rapid strewn-field prediction plus standard landowner-permission contracts and a fresh-fall sales channel for meteorite hunters, extendable to satellite-debris reentries.
customer: Serious hunters and dealers (subscription), landowners and park districts (permission desks), and buyers of fresh-fall specimens.
problem: The 17 March 2026 Ohio fall drew swarms of hunters, with pieces going for roughly $400-500 per gram early on, while a golf club closed its property and a park district warned hunters off. Permission takes days, fresh-fall value decays fast, and there is no standard revenue share with landowners.
solution: Alerts within 30-60 minutes combining public bolide and radar data with hobby camera networks and automated strewn maps. A pre-registered hunter roster with waivers, a standard landowner-share contract signed digitally, on-site chain of custody, classification via a partner lab, and consignment to dealers and museums.
why_now: The Ohio fall made the economics and the access conflict public. Open satellite and radar data and cheap all-sky cameras exist, and Starlink reentries add a second, insurer-relevant use case.
revenue_model: $20/month alerts, 10-15% of specimen sales, landowner-desk fees from park districts and insurers, and data licensing.
non_obvious_insight: Strewn-field maps are already published free, so the scarce thing is access and legitimacy in the first 72 hours. A contract-and-permission layer turns hostile landowners into revenue partners and creates an exclusive right-of-entry that cannot be scraped.
first_30_days: Build a 200-person hunter Discord and draft a standard landowner agreement. Test it on the next reported fireball with 20 landowners, and sign 2 dealers to buy through the network.

title: ITAR-Safe Identity for New-Space Startups
one_liner: An identity layer that proves a new hire is real, where they actually are and whether they may legally see spacecraft technical data, then feeds that attribute straight into SSO and PLM access controls.
customer: Series A-C launch, satellite and defense-space startups (50-500 staff) and their sub-tier machine shops and avionics suppliers, reached through space-focused investors, accelerators and SpaceWERX/SBIR cohorts. Buyers are the head of security or compliance and the CFO.
problem: Space startups are hiring at breakneck speed, with remote engineers and contractors, into a Golden Dome-driven market (cost estimate raised to $185B) and nine-figure funding rounds. Giving a foreign person access to technical data is an ITAR export violation, and North Korean IT-worker schemes have reached 70 to 100+ US companies. Standard IDV proves someone is real, not whether they are a US person, and HR and ATS tools do not carry export-control eligibility as an access attribute. Fake suppliers and counterfeit parts add a second exposure.
solution: (1) Verify person and US-person status using document and injection-resistant liveness (partner with an existing IDV vendor rather than building it). (2) Check presence over time (VPN and laptop-farm signals). (3) Write 'US person, permitted data categories' into Okta or Entra groups and PLM and repo permissions through SCIM. (4) Supplier onboarding with KYB, sanctions and counterfeit-part red flags. (5) An auditor-ready evidence pack for CMMC Level 2 assessments and export-compliance reviews.
why_now: The DoD's CMMC rollout reaches its second phase on 10 Nov 2026, when third-party Level 2 certification starts appearing in contracts, and small suppliers are scrambling. North Korean worker prosecutions in Apr and May 2026 put hiring fraud on boards' agendas, while 3-second voice cloning and virtual-camera injection attacks defeat casual video interviews.
revenue_model: $60-120 per verified person per year, $1-3K per month platform fee, and $250 per supplier onboarding. Add a paid $2K 'ITAR access audit' as an entry product.
non_obvious_insight: In space the compliance object is not employee identity but nationality-scoped access to technical data. The unbuilt gap is attribute-based access control fed by identity proof into CAD and PLM systems. These startups fear DDTC and DoD audits and investor diligence more than hackers, so they buy compliance evidence rather than security.
first_30_days: Build a 'verified US person to Okta group' integration on an off-the-shelf IDV API. Sell a $2K ITAR access audit (export the Drive, GitHub and PLM permission lists and flag foreign-person exposures) to 5 startups via investor and accelerator introductions in Colorado Springs, Los Angeles and Huntsville. Convert audits to per-seat subscriptions before the Nov 2026 CMMC milestone.

title: Safe-Deposit Box Successor With Heir Protocol
one_liner: A bonded, insured vault subscription for original wills, deeds, titles, seed-phrase backups and heirlooms, with a scripted release protocol for heirs, sold through estate attorneys as the bank box disappears.
customer: Estate-planning and elder-law attorneys as the channel, and their clients aged 55 to 85 whose plan says 'the original is in the safe deposit box'. Secondary: coin, gold and crypto holders, and small landlords and business owners holding original deeds and titles.
problem: Chase said in August 2025 that it would phase out all remaining safe deposit boxes nationwide, after it stopped new rentals in 2021. Capital One, Santander and Citizens exited earlier, and the total number of boxes has reportedly fallen from about 40M to an estimated 25M to 32M. Contents are not FDIC-insured, and no federal law governs boxes. On a death the bank typically freezes access until paperwork clears. The box was the default chain of custody for the paper that proves who owns what, and nothing has replaced it.
solution: Rent standardized boxes or sealed envelopes inside licensed, bonded vault partners. Each item gets a photo and hash inventory, and contents are insured under a valuables policy. The core product is a designated-heir protocol: on a death certificate plus an attorney letter or executor's letters, the vault releases to the named person after video attestation and dual control. Add periodic proof-of-life check-ins, an index the attorney can see, and an original-will custody service tied to the attorney's office.
why_now: Chase's nationwide phase-out (announced August 2025) removed the largest holder of boxes. The Great Wealth Transfer is under way. Retail gold and crypto holdings create new 'irreplaceable original' items such as seed backups and coins that people do not want in a home closet.
revenue_model: $15 to $35 per month per box, or $199 to $399 per year. A $99 onboarding and inventory fee. A $250 heir-release fee. A white-label or referral share of $5 to $10 per client per month for law firms. Margin on the insurance premium.
non_obvious_insight: The box was never about valuables. It was legal chain of custody for original paper, and banks are quitting because vault space is expensive real estate, not because the need went away. The product is the death protocol that banks never offered, since banks freeze access and a vault plus an attorney workflow can release to the named heir within days. Attorneys are the distribution because they carry malpractice risk when originals are lost.
first_30_days: Check whether your state regulates safe-deposit companies, then sign a white-label deal with one existing bonded vault or secure records-storage operator in a single metro. Draft the release protocol and client agreement with two estate attorneys. Present to 5 estate-planning firms and one senior center with a free 'Where are your originals?' inventory worksheet as the lead magnet. Sell 30 founding-member boxes at a discounted annual rate and run the first two mock heir releases to prove the protocol.

title: Insurer-Funded Chronic Care for Diabetic Pets
one_liner: A tech-led diabetes and kidney-disease program for insured pets, paid per member per month by insurers who capture the avoided ER claims.
customer: Mid-size pet insurers and MGAs (for example Fetch, Pumpkin, Odie and Lassie-type carriers) that need to cut claim severity. Independent clinics are the referral partner, and self-pay owners are the fallback.
problem: Diabetes and kidney disease in cats and dogs generate $3-6K a year in claims and emergency DKA admissions. AAHA's 2026 guidelines emphasize CGMs and once-daily insulins, but the workflow of monitoring, titration, coaching and refills has no owner. Vets are overloaded, vet techs are 2 per vet against a 4:1 ideal, and insurers' premiums are up 19.7% against animals up 9%, so they need to reduce claim costs rather than only raise prices.
solution: Sell insurers a PMPM disease-management pod: CGM starter kit, weekly data review by licensed vet techs under a supervising vet via the owner's clinic, protocol-driven insulin titration messages, refill logistics, and early-warning routing to the clinic before DKA. Enrollment is found in the insurer's claims file. Clinics are paid a titration-visit fee so they are not disintermediated. Insurers pay $40-70 PMPM with shared savings on avoided ER events.
why_now: AAHA split canine and feline diabetes guidelines in 2026 and put CGMs at the center. CGMs and long-acting insulins are arriving at once. Ambient AI and the vet-tech underuse make labor arbitrage possible. Insurers face repricing backlash, and remote VCPR rules are loosening piecemeal.
revenue_model: PMPM from insurers, gain-share on avoided claims, and CGM sensor and supply margin. Owner self-pay at $59 a month as a fallback.
non_obvious_insight: Insurers sit on the only longitudinal dataset and carry the financial downside. Clinics hold the license but not the time. This is Livongo-style economics: the payer who owns the downside pays for prevention, and vet techs are the labor arbitrage. Chronic care is a claims-cost product, not a telehealth product.
first_30_days: Convince one small MGA to share a de-identified diabetic-claims cohort and pilot a 200-pet program at cost. Recruit two RVTs and a supervising vet. If insurers are slow, launch a $59 a month owner-pay version through 5 clinics to get outcome data within 90-120 days.

title: Drone-Ready Rx Lockers as Adherence Infrastructure
one_liner: A lockable, temperature-buffered, authenticated receiving station at a senior's home that accepts drone or courier drops and quietly reports whether the medication was retrieved.
customer: Medicare Advantage plans and pharmacy chains, paying per active station plus per delivery. Independent-living communities are the pilot channel.
problem: Drone delivery is scaling (Wing/Walmart 270+ sites by 2027, Lowe's launch on Sep 28, 2026), but a 78-year-old cannot reliably receive a 2.5 lb drop. Bending, theft, weather and controlled-substance rules get in the way. Plans lose Star Ratings money on medication non-adherence, and solo agers have no daily check-in.
solution: A roughly $120 bill-of-materials box (porch, balcony or window mounted) with recipient authentication, insulation and a retrieval sensor. Start with human courier deliveries into the same locker, and add drone-network integration as it opens. A missed-retrieval alert goes to the pharmacy, then the family.
why_now: Retail drone networks are now big enough to need a receiving standard. Part D adherence measures are triple-weighted in Star Ratings. Medicare Advantage benefit cuts (OTC benefits from 9.6% to 2.4% of plans) push plans to look for outcome-linked spend.
revenue_model: $8-15 per month per station from plans or pharmacies, plus a per-retrieval fee to drone operators or pharmacies. Optional hardware financing.
non_obvious_insight: The delivery event is the cheapest, least creepy daily proof-of-life signal, and no camera or wearable is needed. The receiving end, not the flight, is the missing piece of senior drone delivery.
first_30_days: Build 20 units. Place them in two independent-living communities where the operator controls the landing zone. Sign an independent pharmacy chain for human-courier deliveries. Bring adherence and retrieval data to one MA plan's pharmacy team.

title: The Weekly Mail Box for Mom
one_liner: A prepaid return envelope where a parent drops all her mail. It gets scanned, triaged, shredded, and turned into a 'what needs doing' digest for her adult child.
customer: Adult children aged 45-62 with a parent 75+ living alone, often 100+ miles away. Secondary customers are daily money managers, professional fiduciaries and elder-law firms who currently collect and read mail by hand.
problem: Paper mail is where scams (fake invoices, 'prize fees', Medicare plan pitches), real bills and the notices that cost money arrive: property-tax exemption renewals, Part D changes, IRS notices, Medicaid paperwork. Kids discover the unopened shoebox at Thanksgiving. USPS Informed Delivery shows only the exterior of some letter-size mail. Parents refuse apps, dashboards and shared passwords because that feels like surrender.
solution: A weekly pre-addressed return flat that the parent fills with the whole pile, with no sorting. The team scans it, uses AI to classify and extract sender, amount, due date and required action, flags likely scams (any 'send a check to claim your prize' letter), and calls or texts the parent for urgent items ('Do you want the water bill paid?'). The child gets a weekly digest and a dashboard. Originals are shredded or returned monthly, per the parent's choice. Over time it builds the 'where everything is' paper trail that estates need: accounts, policies, pensions and annuities.
why_now: Cheap, accurate AI document extraction only became affordable at consumer prices in the last two years. Treasury phased out paper checks on Sept 30, 2025, and agencies are pushing digital, while seniors still get paper notices. Older-adult scam losses run in the billions per year (FTC). Medicare open enrollment begins Oct 15, so the mailer flood is imminent.
revenue_model: $49/month per household (about $14 in postage, scanning and AI, for roughly 70% gross margin). $25 per household per month wholesale for daily money managers and fiduciaries. Optional $149 one-time 'estate paper trail' report.
non_obvious_insight: Seniors will turn down every dashboard, but they will hand over an envelope pile happily, because mailing is a ritual they own. The pile is the real system of record for a widow's finances. Scam checks and wire requests are usually triggered by letters, so scanning the inside of the envelope catches what exterior-only tools cannot. Children do not want passwords either. They want to know what to pay.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 households in one metro through caregiver Facebook groups, local AARP caregiver meetings and elder-law attorneys. Run it manually with a $500 duplex scanner, an AI extraction pipeline and a retired teacher doing quality checks. Charge from day one. Track 'catches' (scams intercepted, missed notices found) and publish them. Then pitch daily money managers.

title: Passive-Radar Drone Detection for Prisons
one_liner: Detect small drones by listening to ambient cell, broadcast and Wi-Fi signals, with no transmitter, no license and no radar permit.
customer: State departments of corrections, county jails, and secondary customers such as critical infrastructure and stadiums.
problem: Cape Canaveral radars see aircraft up to a 747 but not a quadcopter. State prisons face contraband drops with low budgets and cannot deploy active radar or jammers. Remote ID and RF detection miss drones that are not broadcasting.
solution: A rooftop kit of low-cost software-defined radios using the signal reflections of existing cell towers and broadcast transmitters, with ML-based detection of small-drone Doppler signatures. It alerts a mobile app and logs evidence for prosecution, and it is passive so legal risk is minimal.
why_now: Cheap SDRs and modern ML make passive sensing of low-cross-section targets feasible in 2025-26. Small-drone detection is now flagged as thin even at major federal sites, and drone traffic is exploding with 200,000-unit purchases (verify feasibility and prison contraband scale).
revenue_model: $25-60K per site installation plus $500-1,500 per month for software and monitoring.
non_obvious_insight: Passivity is the business model. Local agencies cannot legally emit RF or mitigate, so a purely receiving sensor is the only kind they can buy without federal permission.
first_30_days: Recruit one university RF lab. Pilot on a rooftop with an existing tower nearby and log real drone passes. Approach 3 state corrections security chiefs for a paid pilot.

title: Municipal Trade Crews as Robot Training Data
one_liner: A cooperative that licenses consented, privacy-scrubbed first-person footage of city public-works and utility crews doing real skilled work to robotics labs, with revenue shared to the city and the union's training fund.
customer: Robotics foundation-model labs and robot-data buyers pay per usable hour (Physical Intelligence-class labs, XDOF, Mecka). The supply side is public works departments, transit maintenance shops and public-sector union locals (AFSCME, IBEW), which receive a 40-50% share.
problem: The humanoid bottleneck is a 'dearth of physical-world data'. Robot-data startups pay people to film themselves making coffee or fixing cars (XDOF at about $50M annualized revenue three months out of stealth, Mecka projecting $100M ARR). Those demos are shallow next to expert skilled-trade work in messy environments: valve exercising, hydrant flushing, pothole patching, streetlight repair, sewer inspection. Cities meanwhile face tight budgets and need non-tax revenue.
solution: Equip volunteer crews with head cameras and simple sensors for specified tasks. Scrub faces and license plates on-device, label task steps, and license clean hours under a contract in which the city retains ownership. Worker pay per hour and a union-controlled training fund keep labor onside. Later, offer 'task-specific corpora' by trade (electrical, plumbing, HVAC) via apprenticeship programs.
why_now: Robot foundation models raised at $3-14B valuations in 2026 and are starved for data. Data-as-a-service is the hot new category (XDOF, Mecka). The humanoid shipment wave (about 22,000 in H1 2026) creates immediate demand. Cities are under budget pressure (Maryland's new IT tax raised 77% less than projected).
revenue_model: Data licensing per usable hour and per task-specific corpus, with 40-50% of revenue shared to the city and union training fund. Enterprise annual data licenses for labs.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input for physical AI is expert skilled-trades demonstrations, and public works departments and their unions are the only large organized pools of trained workers with a single governance body that can sign one contract. Paying the workers and the union turns what looks like 'training your replacement' into a data dividend.
first_30_days: Find one mid-size public works department and one union local. Run a 10-worker, 2-week pilot with head cameras on two task types. Sell the first 300-500 cleaned hours to one robotics lab and pay the crews and training fund on the first invoice.

title: Offline Distilled Agent Box for Denied Networks
one_liner: Ruggedized GPU box that runs small models distilled from a unit's own GenAI.mil agents, with zero connectivity.
customer: National Guard and reserve units, Army and Marine tactical staffs, border and disaster-response agencies, and defense integrators serving units in disconnected or denied environments.
problem: GenAI.mil is unclassified only and needs connectivity, yet users built more than 100k custom agents. The CDAO says compute is the binding constraint, and classified models cannot train in commercial data centers. Units in the field cannot use any of it.
solution: A service that takes a unit's approved agent workflows on GenAI.mil, distills them into small open-weight models with tool wrappers, and ships them on a rugged 1-2 GPU box with a one-screen interface. It updates by sneakernet with signed model bundles.
why_now: Open-weight small models are now good enough for narrow tasks. Right-sizing to cut inference cost is an explicit DoD priority, and model-vendor politics make owning a portable, vendor-independent model attractive.
revenue_model: $40-90K per box and $2-5K per month for update and distillation services. Government pilot funding via SBIR or CSO awards.
non_obvious_insight: The 100k user-built agents are an unwritten requirements document for what warfighters want. The winner distills the demand signal, not the model.
first_30_days: Ask 3 Guard units for one repetitive workflow (maintenance triage, reporting). Build a demo on commodity hardware with an open-weight model. Apply for one SBIR topic and ask an integrator for a paid subcontract.

title: Supplier-Funded Books for Trade-Credit Customers
one_liner: Regional distributors pay to give each micro-customer done-for-you books, and get a permissioned live view of that customer's credit risk.
customer: Regional wholesale distributors (foodservice, produce, beauty supply, auto parts, building materials, uniform and linen) with 500-10,000 micro accounts on net-30 terms.
problem: Distributors extend trade credit to taquerias, salons and garages on gut feel, and bad debt and slow pay eat margin. Micro-customers keep no books, so there is no data to underwrite against. Ramp and Brex have moved upmarket and no vendor serves this tier. The owners will not pay for bookkeeping themselves.
solution: Every active account gets free, done-for-you books, funded by the distributor. Bank and card feeds are connected, the distributor's own invoices are auto-ingested, and receipts arrive by text or WhatsApp. The customer owns the ledger and can export it any time. With the customer's opt-in, the distributor sees cash coverage, the aging of the customer's other bills and payment-risk flags, and can raise limits or offer early-pay discounts to accounts that look healthy.
why_now: LLM categorization pushes cost per account below about $10 a month. The Fed's 2026 data shows microfirms are cash-tight (22% of applicants got no financing, and nonemployers lean on personal funds). The Bench collapse made data ownership and portability a selling point.
revenue_model: The distributor pays $10-25 per active account per month, justified by bad-debt reduction, shorter DSO and lower churn. Upsells: tax filing, payroll, and early-payment financing with a revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: The micro-business will never pay for bookkeeping, but the party carrying its receivable will. A bad account costs a distributor thousands, while $15 a month is noise. Sponsorship also raises switching costs, so the distributor gets retention for free.
first_30_days: Pick one vertical in one metro, such as a produce or beauty-supply distributor. Get 12 months of invoices and payment history for 100 accounts, then backtest whether simple books-derived signals predict late payment. Sign a paid pilot covering 100 accounts, with success defined as DSO and write-offs.

title: Off-Market Farmland Transfer Radar
one_liner: Score farm parcels likely to change hands through estates before they are ever listed.
customer: Farmland brokers, ag lenders, farmland REITs, land-buying farm groups and ag estate attorneys.
problem: Listing data shows only the visible market, but about a third of landlords are 75 or older, only about 1 in 4 farmers has a succession plan, and millions of acres will move through estates.
solution: Combine public probate filings, assessor and ownership records and landlord-age modeling into county-level parcel transfer scores and alerts, sold by subscription.
why_now: The 2026 reporting on the invisible farmland transfer and a multi-year farm-income squeeze mean lenders and buyers want early visibility into forced and estate sales.
revenue_model: County-pack subscriptions of $300-1,500/month, plus success fees to brokers and lenders on originated deals.
non_obvious_insight: The biggest land flow is invisible to listing-based data, and the underlying records are public but fragmented county by county. Data plumbing rather than model quality is the moat.
first_30_days: Scrape probate and assessor data in three Midwest counties, build a first transfer-likelihood score, and pitch 15 local brokers and two ag lenders on a paid pilot.

title: Inherited Low-Rate Mortgage Concierge for Heirs
one_liner: A flat-fee service that helps heirs keep, assume or transfer a parent's low-rate mortgage instead of paying it off at closing, and values that rate as an estate asset so siblings can buy each other out fairly.
customer: Heirs (Gen X, aged 45-60) who inherit a home with a mortgage at 3-4% while new loans cost about 7.5%. The estate attorneys, probate realtors and bank trust officers who advise them refer clients and pay for tooling.
problem: The default estate path is to sell the house and pay off the loan, which destroys below-market financing. On a $300K balance at about 3.25% with 22 years left versus 7.5%, the rate is worth roughly $90K in present value (my calculation). Federal rules generally bar lenders from calling loans due on transfer to relatives at death, and confirmed successors have servicing rights under CFPB rules, but servicers are slow and inconsistent and heirs do not know. Siblings often cannot buy each other out at current rates, and a buyer's market with concessions on 44.7% of sales makes forced sales costlier.
solution: Within days of a death, verify loan type, rate, balance and assumability and confirm successor-in-interest status with the servicer. Bridge payments during probate, and produce a Rate Asset Report that values the rate for the estate inventory so heirs can split fairly. Structure buyouts with junior notes or partner lenders so one heir keeps or rents the house, and for sellers show where FHA or VA assumability lifts the sale price. Confirm applicability with counsel, since protections generally cover owner-occupied 1-4 unit homes.
why_now: Rates are rising again (Redfin: futures price the Fed funds rate at 5% by end-2027, and the 30-year is about 7.4-7.6%). A large share of Boomer mortgages sit below 4%, and the first wave of the transfer is arriving. Record concessions make selling into this market expensive. ROAD to Housing Act limits on institutional single-family owners push heirs to be small landlords.
revenue_model: $1,500-2,500 flat fee per estate or a share of rate-value preserved, a $499 Rate Asset Report, referral fees from buyout lenders, and $200 per month tooling subscriptions for probate attorneys.
non_obvious_insight: The great wealth transfer is counted in balance-sheet dollars, but in a 7.5% world the most valuable asset in many middle-class estates is the interest rate on the parent's mortgage, and the default estate process throws it away at closing.
first_30_days: Write servicer letter templates and an assumability checklist reviewed by an attorney. Recruit five probate attorneys and three probate realtors. Launch the $499 Rate Asset Report to estates with mortgages and track how many convert to the full service. Sign one HELOC or non-QM lender as buyout-financing partner.

title: Scan-Before-Buyout: Digital Memory and Game Assets
one_liner: Capture homes and streets in flood buyouts and burn zones in game-engine-grade 3D before demolition. The program pays for compliance and memorial; asset licensing to games and film is upside.
customer: County and state hazard-mitigation offices running buyouts, their historic-preservation consultants, and community foundations or long-term recovery groups funding memorials. Secondary buyers are game studios, VFX houses and XR training vendors.
problem: Buyouts demolish hundreds of 50-year-old homes. Federal funding triggers historic-property review, and the mitigation is often recorded documentation costing thousands per structure and producing a binder nobody opens. Families lose the physical record of their home and street, and the neighborhood dissolves undocumented. Only about 13% of affected Palisades owners have started rebuilding, so many lots sit for years. Game and film studios pay for authentic real-world environments that are hard to source.
solution: A crew of ex-game and VFX 3D artists uses Gaussian-splat or photogrammetry capture to scan exteriors, streetscapes and, with owner consent, interiors in an afternoon per home. Deliverables: (a) a compliance-grade documentation package, (b) a walkable keepsake file for each family, and (c) a de-identified 'American small-town' building kit licensed to studios, with revenue share to the community memorial fund.
why_now: Post-2024/25 flood buyouts are reaching demolition, and BRIC's $1B was reinstated in March 2026. Capture cost collapsed with splatting tools and phone-grade scanning. Game and VFX layoffs put skilled 3D artists on the market (Ubisoft headcount fell from 18,666 to 16,590 and EA's new owners plan AI-driven cost cuts), while studios need cheaper environment art.
revenue_model: Government or foundation contracts of $1,500-4,000 per structure or $40-150K per neighborhood, an optional $49 family keepsake often paid by a recovery fund, and five-figure per-studio licenses for the asset kit with revenue share to the county.
non_obvious_insight: The compliance mandate pays the bills, not the games market. Creative-industry tooling makes a documentation chore that nobody enjoys far cheaper, and turns it into a bereavement product and a licensable asset library. The county gets a better deliverable and a revenue share instead of a cost center.
first_30_days: Offer a free pilot street of 10 homes to a buyout manager in a post-flood region (western North Carolina or the Texas Hill Country). Collect owner releases. Deliver the splats plus a template mitigation stipulation a state preservation office can accept. Sell an anonymized kit on Fab, Sketchfab or the Unity store to test demand. Pitch consulting firms for subcontract work and a community foundation for the memorial grant.

title: Certified SDE for Sub-$1M Business Sales
one_liner: A CPA-signed, AI-prepared earnings certificate that lets brokers, buyers and SBA lenders trust a small business's seller's discretionary earnings.
customer: Business brokers, SBA lenders and first-time buyers in $100k-$1M main-street deals, and the sellers who pay to be believed.
problem: A full quality-of-earnings review costs $15-50k, which is impossible on a $300k deal, so cash-heavy books and owner add-backs create distrust. Deals die in diligence or stall in lender underwriting. Search funds target $5-50M businesses and nothing standardizes trust for the smallest tier.
solution: Upload three years of returns, bank and processor statements and POS data. The system reconstructs revenue, recasts SDE with add-back evidence, and flags unrecorded revenue or personal expenses. A CPA signs a certified SDE range in 48 hours. Partner lenders accept the standard report, and it links to the escrow and route-sale flow.
why_now: SBA 7(a) plus 504 financing up to $10M began July 2026, so buyer demand and lender appetite are rising. LLMs and bank data make the reconstruction cheap.
revenue_model: $495-995 per report paid by the seller or broker, lender licensing, and buyer diligence upsells.
non_obvious_insight: At this size the bottleneck is neither buyers nor capital but trust in the earnings number. A QoE costs 5% of price, and a cheap certificate unlocks the whole tier.
first_30_days: Sign three brokers who list $200k-800k deals and produce 15 reports manually with a CPA. Ask one SBA lender in writing what it needs in order to accept the certificate.

title: Heirloom Fair-Division Engine for Sibling Estates
one_liner: Use a fair-division algorithm and a phone walkthrough to split a dead parent's belongings so nobody feels cheated.
customer: Executors (often the eldest child), estate attorneys, mediators and professional fiduciaries. Families pay $149-$399 per estate, or attorneys pay $99/month.
problem: Research on inheritance conflict (for example the University of Minnesota's 'Who Gets Grandma's Yellow Pie Plate?' work) finds sentimental personal property, not money, triggers most sibling fights. Executors improvise with turn-taking or a spreadsheet, distant siblings get shortchanged, and the house can't be sold until it is cleared.
solution: A phone walkthrough captures the house room by room, AI tags items, and each remote heir gets a private points budget to express wants. A fair-division algorithm (adjusted-winner or envy-free-up-to-one-item style) proposes an allocation with cash or point equalization. The app then coordinates shipping and pickup, and routes leftovers to donation with receipts or to sale. It ends with a signed distribution memo the attorney can file. Each item keeps a story card so its history survives.
why_now: Multimodal AI can inventory objects from video, and phone-based 3D capture is mainstream. Boomer households hold decades of belongings that Millennial and Gen X heirs scattered across the country often don't want. With the federal estate tax largely out of the picture for most families (reported $15M exemption), family conflict is the main remaining risk.
revenue_model: Per-estate fee ($149-$399), 10-15% margin on shipping and donation logistics, and attorney seats at $99/month.
non_obvious_insight: The fights are about objects, not dollars. Objects are one of the few asset classes with a known mechanism-design solution, and no estate product uses it.
first_30_days: Build a no-code prototype with a spreadsheet points auction. Offer it free to 20 executors found in estate-help forums and groups. Ask elder-law attorneys to use it as a mediation-lite deliverable and convert 5 of them to paid. Time-box the whole thing to about three weeks per estate.

title: Muthoot-Style Gold Loans for America's Junk Drawers
one_liner: A mail-in, XRF-assayed loan against gold and jewelry at roughly 24-36% APR, versus 200%-plus at a typical US pawn shop, run through licensed pawn partners for people who need $300-$5,000 and have idle gold worth far more with gold trading around $4,100-$4,500 an ounce.
customer: Middle-income households aged 35-65 with jewelry and coins in a drawer and thin or damaged credit who need a few hundred to a few thousand dollars for a car repair, rent gap or tax bill. Small-business owners with a cash-flow gap are the second segment.
problem: Cash-for-gold buyers pay a fraction of melt value with no way to get the piece back. Pawn shops charge 10-25% a month. Payday and title lenders charge triple-digit APRs. The only cheap collateral-backed product is stigmatized, store-based and priced for rent rather than risk, so many people with real assets choose worse options or sell irreplaceable pieces at a loss.
solution: Mail an insured kit (or drop off at a partner pawn store). On receipt, run an XRF assay and weigh, then offer 70-75% of melt value within hours and pay by ACH. Redeem by paying principal plus interest, and the piece comes back insured. If the borrower does not repay, the gold is sold at melt with any surplus returned where state law requires. There is no collections calling and no credit reporting. Interest is about 2% a month falling for repeat borrowers. Hedge the collateral pool with gold futures. Launch through a licensed pawnbroker as lender of record, then license state by state.
why_now: Gold has traded roughly between $4,100 and $4,500 an ounce in September 2026, so a drawer of old 14k jewelry is worth several times what it was in 2022. Indian gold-loan lenders (Muthoot, Rupeek and others) have shown that 9-25% APR gold lending is profitable at scale, while US pawn remains a fragmented, store-based, high-rate market. Cheap XRF analyzers, insured shipping and instant ACH remove the storefront cost that justified those US rates.
revenue_model: Interest of 1.5-2.5% a month on outstanding loans, plus a small handling fee on loans under $500, plus surplus on forfeited gold sold above the loan amount. Funded by a private-credit warehouse line at low double-digit cost of capital. Because loans are 70-75% of a liquid commodity's melt value, credit losses are close to hedging and shipping costs.
non_obvious_insight: The 200%-plus APR of US pawn is not a price for risk, because collateral makes the loss very small. It is a price for store rent, low volume and stigma. Remove the storefront and the mass-market stigma (customers are gold owners with poor liquidity, not desperate borrowers) and you can undercut incumbents 5-8x on price and still earn better returns on capital than a bank.
first_30_days: Sign a licensed pawnbroker in Texas or Florida as lender of record so you inherit their license and compliance, including police reporting of transactions. Buy an XRF analyzer and a rated insured vault or use a custody partner. Raise about $250k to fund the first 50-100 loans. Buy search and social ads that intercept 'sell my gold' intent and publish the true APR up front. First loans should close within 4-6 weeks, and the pilot's default and hedging data becomes the pitch for a credit line.

title: Sold-Out-of-Trust Radar for Floorplan Lenders
one_liner: Catch dealers that sell floored cars and pocket the payoff by watching the one signal an F&I insider knows can't be hidden: the VIN disappears from public listings but the floorplan payoff never arrives.
customer: Floorplan lenders and their auditors: independent floorplan companies, captive finance arms, regional banks and credit unions with dealer lines, and warehouse lenders that fund subprime and buy-here-pay-here dealers. Pay $15 to $30 per monitored dealer per month plus enterprise data fees.
problem: A dealer sells out of trust when it sells a floored car and does not pay the lender's payoff on time. It is how small cash squeezes become fraud. Ford and Stellantis are in court against Sky Auto Mall over exactly this, and floorplan use is heavier with inventory at roughly 88 days' supply and rates at SOFR plus 200 to 400 bps. Lenders police it with periodic on-site audits (monthly, quarterly or random), so a dealer can sell for weeks before anyone looks. The dealer's own delay makes it worse, since contracts in transit stretch to a week or more before the lender funds, so honest and dishonest dealers look identical in the books.
solution: Daily VIN-level monitoring of each lender's floored inventory against public and licensed listing feeds from the dealer's site and the major marketplaces. When a floored VIN disappears from listings, the tool starts a clock. It cross-checks against lender-provided payoff events and, where available, title and registration transactions and electronic lien releases. If no payoff shows within the expected window (about 7 to 10 days for a clean deal, longer for slow lenders), it flags the dealer and VIN and ranks risk by dealer history and how many VINs are in the queue. Flags trigger a spot audit or a curtailment call. A dealer-facing version shows honest dealers exactly which VINs look 'unpaid' so they can fix processing before the lender calls, and it doubles as an early-warning feed for warehouse lenders.
why_now: Sept 2025's Tricolor and PrimaLend collapses put double-pledged collateral and verification failures in front of every subprime lender and their investors. In March 2026 Ford and Stellantis were still litigating floorplan fraud against Sky Auto Mall. Rising inventory and higher rates increase floorplan reliance. Public listing feeds and cheap LLM data extraction make VIN-level monitoring practical for a team of three.
revenue_model: Per-dealer monthly monitoring fee, a per-alert fee on confirmed cases, and enterprise data licensing to captives and ABS or warehouse investors. Upsell: a contracts-in-transit tracker that gives dealers a lender-verified funding timeline and later powers same-day advances against verified contracts.
non_obvious_insight: The only place SOT cannot hide is the retail listing. A dealer will lie about payoffs, backdate titles and pay one lender with another's money, but it still has to take a car off its website when it sells it, because customers and marketplaces punish stale listings. Auditors check what is on the lot; nobody checks what left the internet. An F&I person knows this from watching sold cars vanish from the site the same day the deal is signed, and from knowing how long a funded payoff should really take.
first_30_days: Build a scraper for a pilot set of 50 dealer inventory pages and a listing-history log. Backtest on cases visible in public court filings (the Sky Auto Mall filings and a handful of others) to show the signal would have fired weeks earlier. Approach three small independent floorplan lenders and two credit unions with dealer floorplan lines, offer a free 60-day pilot on their books, and charge $20 per dealer per month after proving at least one real catch.
